activity_mechanics.Agree, Disagree, It Depends: Use a claim with enough nuance for agreement, disagreement or a conditional position. Avoid one-fact questions.
activity_mechanics.Bad Advice Only: Give a realistic problem; the learner must produce intentionally bad advice, then explain why it is bad or repair it.
activity_mechanics.Conversation Roulette: Use varied conversational prompts that can sustain an unscripted exchange and allow follow-up questions.
activity_mechanics.Convince Me: Give a concrete position, product, choice or action the learner must persuade another person to accept.
activity_mechanics.Defend the Opposite: Use a defensible opinion or preference and require the learner to argue for the opposite side.
activity_mechanics.Explain It Without Saying It: Provide a target concept plus forbidden obvious words so the learner must paraphrase.
activity_mechanics.Make It Sound Like a Person: Start from stiff, robotic or over-literal English and require a more natural conversational version.
activity_mechanics.Odd One Out — Conversation Edition: Use four items with one defensible odd item. The distinction should support discussion, not rely on trivial categories.
activity_mechanics.One Minute, No Escape: Give a topic specific enough to sustain one minute of speech without becoming a list of disconnected facts.
activity_mechanics.Repair the Conversation: Provide a conversational breakdown, awkward line or misunderstanding and require a natural repair.
activity_mechanics.Sell Me Something Useless: Give an intentionally unnecessary object or service and require persuasive language and benefits.
activity_mechanics.Story Chain — But Something Changes: Give a story seed and a change/twist that forces the learner to continue coherently.
activity_mechanics.The Missing Detail: Give a statement whose usefulness depends on one or more missing concrete details the learner must identify or add.
activity_mechanics.The Missing Question: Give an answer or conversational fragment and require the learner to infer a natural preceding question.
activity_mechanics.Three Questions Deeper: Start from a normal topic and require three progressively deeper but appropriate follow-up questions.
activity_mechanics.Upgrade That Answer: Give a short, vague or basic answer and require a fuller, more precise, more natural response.
activity_mechanics.What Happened Just Before?: Give a moment or outcome with enough clues for the learner to infer plausible immediately preceding events.
activity_mechanics.Would You Rather — No Easy Answers: Offer two plausible options with a real trade-off so the learner must justify a choice.
activity_mechanics.Take a Side: Use a clear proposition with two plausible positions and require a reasoned stance.
activity_mechanics.Change My Mind: Give a position held by the teacher/listener; the learner must challenge it with reasons, examples and reframing.
activity_mechanics.The Better Question: Provide a weak, vague or closed question and require a more useful, natural or revealing question.
activity_mechanics.What Would You Say?: Give a concrete social or professional situation with a clear communicative purpose.
activity_mechanics.Say It Three Ways: Use one meaning or intention that can be expressed naturally in three different registers, tones or phrasings.
activity_mechanics.Keep It Going: Give a short conversational exchange at risk of ending; the learner must extend it naturally.
activity_mechanics.The Awkward Silence: Create a realistic silence after a remark or event; the learner must restart or redirect the conversation.
activity_mechanics.What's the Problem?: Provide symptoms, clues or a situation from which the learner can identify and explain the underlying problem.
activity_mechanics.You Have 30 Seconds: Use a compact speaking task with one clear objective that can be completed under time pressure.
activity_mechanics.One Detail Is False: Give a compact set of personal-style details where one can plausibly be false; the learner must question or infer.
Give a category and meaningful criteria so the learner must design, prioritise and justify an ideal version.
activity_mechanics.Trade-Off: Present two benefits/costs that cannot all be maximised; require a choice and justification.
activity_mechanics.Emergency English: Use urgent but safe everyday situations where the learner must communicate essential information clearly and quickly.
activity_mechanics.The Complaint Ladder: Start with a service problem and require escalation from polite report to firmer complaint while staying appropriate.
activity_mechanics.Don’t Say Yes: Ask questions designed to trigger agreement, but the learner must respond without simply saying yes and must elaborate.
activity_mechanics.Five Whys: Use a preference, decision or opinion that can deepen through repeated why questions without becoming intrusive.
activity_mechanics.Make It More Specific: Start vague; the learner must add evidence, examples, behaviour, numbers or precise language.
activity_mechanics.Finish My Thought: Provide a sentence stem that naturally produces a complete personal or hypothetical thought.
activity_mechanics.What Are You Assuming?: Use a claim with identifiable hidden assumptions; the task is to surface and question them.
activity_mechanics.Unpopular Opinion: Use low-stakes, non-inflammatory topics; the challenge is argument quality rather than provocation.
activity_mechanics.Explain the Difference: Use a close lexical or conceptual pair and require contexts/examples, not dictionary definitions alone.
activity_mechanics.Which One Sounds More Natural?: Provide understandable alternatives where idiomaticity, collocation or register differs.
activity_mechanics.The Forbidden Easy Word: Ban obvious easy words in a way that forces more precise language while leaving the task achievable.
activity_mechanics.Use These 3 Chunks: Give three chunks that can naturally coexist in one coherent response or exchange.
activity_mechanics.Personalise It: Give a generic statement or example that the learner must turn into a concrete personal or invented example.
activity_mechanics.Guess My Rule: Provide examples that obey a precise hidden rule. teacher_note must state the rule clearly for the teacher.
activity_mechanics.Who Said It?: Give one line containing clues about relationship, context, intention or register; require inference.
activity_mechanics.Before / During / After: Use an event with meaningful preparation, live action and follow-up phases.
activity_mechanics.Problem → Options → Decision: Require problem definition, at least three options, comparison and a justified decision.
activity_mechanics.Interrupt Me Politely: Give an exact reason to interrupt such as clarification, correction, redirect, timing or decision.
activity_mechanics.Tell Me What I Mean: Use indirect language whose intended meaning depends on context, tone or relationship.
activity_mechanics.Bad Small Talk / Good Small Talk: Contrast conversation mechanics rather than wrong grammar versus correct grammar. Format text with explicit BAD: and GOOD: sections so the presenter can render separate cards.
activity_mechanics.Describe Without Adjectives: Choose a target describable through behaviour, actions, events or sensory detail without adjectives.
activity_mechanics.Make It Less Direct: Start needlessly forceful and require softer language while preserving clarity.
activity_mechanics.Make It More Direct: Start too vague or hedged and require clearer language without making it rude.
activity_mechanics.Conversation Fork: Give one conversational moment plus two or three genuinely different strategic directions.
activity_mechanics.The Unexpected Follow-Up: Use a familiar first question plus a second question that forces a new angle rather than simply asking why.
activity_mechanics.Explain Your Choice to Someone Who Disag: Define the listener's competing value so the learner must reframe rather than repeat the same reason.
activity_mechanics.Micro Roleplay: Use one scenario and one objective for roughly 60–90 seconds; the challenge may complicate but must not replace the task.
activity_mechanics.Phrase Auction: Provide five to seven phrases of different usefulness or register. Weak options do not all need to be ungrammatical.
activity_mechanics.Conversation Detective: Give a short dialogue fragment with clues; require inference about relationship, backstory and likely next step.
activity_mechanics.Number Mission: Use consequential numbers inside a two-person information check. The learner must confirm, repeat or repair details rather than simply read numbers aloud.
activity_mechanics.Picture Detective: Use three to six meaningful images. The learner asks questions, describes visible features and identifies a secret picture without the secret leaking into learner-visible data.
activity_mechanics.Make the Choice: Present two to four defensible options with comparable details. The learner chooses, explains priorities and adapts when the teacher reveals a new condition.
activity_mechanics.Quick Pick: Give two to four concrete options that can be chosen quickly. Require one short reason so the game remains speaking-first even at A0/A1.
activity_mechanics.Ask to Unlock: The teacher holds one hidden answer. The learner unlocks it by asking a small number of useful questions. Teacher-only information must stay in teacher_note.
activity_mechanics.Oops, Fix Me!: Show the learner the correct information and let the teacher deliberately say one or two details incorrectly. The learner repairs the mismatch naturally.
activity_mechanics.Build My Day: Show three to five timed actions. The learner turns them into a spoken sequence using time and ordering language, then adapts if one event changes.
activity_mechanics.Three Clues: Give one target and three concrete clues. The learner uses the clues to describe the target in short connected language while the teacher guesses.
activity_mechanics.What Changed?: Show a clear BEFORE and AFTER state. The learner identifies and verbalises the change, then may explain a reason or consequence.
activity_mechanics.Mini Map Mission: Give a start point, destination and a few landmarks. The learner asks for or gives a short route using basic direction language.
activity_mechanics.Pass It Back: Teacher asks one safe everyday question. The learner answers and then keeps the interaction alive by asking one connected question back.
activity_mechanics.Tiny Story Builder: Give WHO, WHERE and ACTION cards. The learner connects them into a tiny coherent story rather than listing the three elements.
activity_mechanics.Which One Fits?: Give one concrete situation and two to four possible phrases. The learner chooses the most natural/appropriate phrase and says it aloud.

# Sblocco Inglese — Speaking Library Item Authoring Guide

This file is the canonical instruction set for generating, reviewing and importing new items into the admin Speaking Library.

The goal is not to create generic conversation questions. Every item must activate a specific speaking behaviour: explaining, reacting, negotiating, repairing, asking, persuading, narrating, clarifying, adapting register, or managing a conversation.

## 1. Non-negotiable principles

1. Speaking first. An item must create meaningful spoken output, not worksheet behaviour.
2. One clear mechanism per game. New items must respect the game mechanic instead of turning every activity into a normal discussion question.
3. Multiple CEFR levels are allowed and encouraged. levels is always an array. An item may be ["A2","B1"], ["B1","B2","C1"], etc.
4. Level means usable speaking demand, not vocabulary prestige. Do not label an item C1 simply because it contains an advanced word.
5. Student-facing text must be immediately understandable on screen.
6. Teacher notes may contain expected answers, hidden information, likely language, correction notes or facilitation advice.
7. Support must help without answering.
8. Challenges must change the speaking demand, not merely say “speak more”.
9. Avoid textbook sameness. Prefer situations, trade-offs, interaction and follow-up over broad prompts.
10. Do not manufacture novelty by swapping nouns. If the same response path works almost unchanged, it is probably the same item.

## 2. Item JSON contract

Every generated item should use this shape:

    {
      "text": "The complete prompt/scenario shown to the student.",
      "levels": ["B1", "B2"],
      "student_support": "Optional scaffold visible to the learner.",
      "challenge": "Optional second-stage complication/reveal.",
      "teacher_note": "Private note, solution, expected interpretation or facilitation cue.",
      "context_tags": ["work", "meeting"],
      "language_targets": ["disagreement", "hedging"],
      "difficulty": 3
    }

Required:
- text: non-empty and presentation-ready.
- levels: one or more of A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2.
- context_tags: 1–4 short lowercase tags.
- language_targets: 1–4 short lowercase tags.
- difficulty: integer 1–5.

Expected when useful:
- student_support: a route into the task without giving the answer.
- challenge: a second reveal that materially deepens the speaking task.
- teacher_note: solutions, hidden context, likely chunks, ambiguity notes, or facilitation advice.

## 3. Context tags

Prefer stable reusable tags before inventing synonyms:

work, career, meeting, client, management, team, supplier, business, interview, study, learning, travel, airport, hotel, transport, restaurant, service, shopping, housing, money, technology, communication, small-talk, social, relationships, conflict, daily-life, habits, food, hobbies, places, personal, story, values, decision, planning, leadership, feedback, negotiation, formal, pragmatics.

Add a new context tag only if none of these reasonably describes the scenario.

## 4. Language targets

Examples:

questions, follow-up, reactions, extended-answer, storytelling, past-simple, past-tenses, present-perfect, conditionals, comparatives, requests, complaints, refusals, disagreement, agreement, hedging, softening, assertiveness, clarification, repair, negotiation, persuasion, rebuttal, concession, register, pragmatics, indirectness, chunks, phrasal-verbs, collocations, lexical-range, precision, plain-English, topic-development, topic-shift, sequencing, problem-solving, prioritisation, trade-offs, inference, speculation, critical-thinking.

These are pedagogical functions, not random vocabulary topics.

## 5. Difficulty scale

- 1 — immediate: concrete, familiar, little ambiguity, minimal planning.
- 2 — supported: familiar situation but requires reason/example/follow-up.
- 3 — flexible: requires adaptation, comparison, complication or sustained interaction.
- 4 — demanding: requires nuance, register control, multiple constraints or perspective shift.
- 5 — high cognitive/pragmatic load: abstract reasoning, stakeholder adaptation, implied meaning, complex negotiation or advanced discourse control.

Difficulty is separate from CEFR. An A2 item can be difficulty 3. A C1 item does not need to be difficulty 5.

## 6. Context-aware novelty / duplicate policy

The application performs an internal novelty check.

### What IS a duplicate

Block or rewrite when:
- normalized text is identical;
- the prompt is a near-paraphrase with the same communicative task;
- context + language target + prompt structure are substantially the same;
- the scenario has only cosmetic substitutions;
- the same answer path would work with almost no adaptation.

Example to reject inside one problem-solving game:
- “Your flight is cancelled. Ask what your options are.”
- “Your train is cancelled. Ask what alternatives you have.”

If the mechanic and response path are identical, replacing flight with train is not enough novelty.

### What is NOT a duplicate

Repeated words are not duplicates by themselves.

The word deadline may legitimately appear in:
- negotiation about changing a deadline;
- storytelling about missing a deadline;
- clarification about what a deadline means;
- a complaint about repeated deadline failures;
- chunk activation containing meet a deadline.

Likewise work, travel, client, manager, good, or a phrasal verb may recur when context or communicative function changes.

### Generator novelty test

Before returning a new item, ask:
1. Is the situation meaningfully different?
2. Is the learner doing a different communicative action?
3. Does it practise a different language target, or the same target in a meaningfully different context?
4. Would the learner need to adapt their answer rather than reuse the same response?
5. Does the new item add coverage to level, context, difficulty or interaction pattern?

If fewer than 2 answers are yes, rewrite the item.

## 7. Batch-generation rules

When generating a batch for one game:
- default batch size: 8–15;
- do not put more than 30% of the batch in the same context;
- include at least 3 distinct context clusters when the game permits it;
- vary difficulty;
- vary item levels;
- avoid putting the hardest item always last;
- avoid repeating the same grammatical frame across the full batch;
- for B1+, include chunks/phrasal verbs where natural, not decoratively;
- do not make all work items corporate-office items;
- do not make all travel items airport/hotel items;
- do not assume every learner is young, single, extroverted, university educated or office-based;
- keep sensitive personal disclosure optional;
- if an item works only because the teacher already knows the answer, place that information in teacher_note.

For 10 items, aim roughly for:
- 2 easier-entry items;
- 5 core items;
- 2 stretch items;
- 1 unusual/high-value item.

## 8. Student support

Good support narrows the route into speaking:
- “Think about timing, cost and convenience.”
- “React first, then ask a connected question.”
- “Choose where you stand on the line, not only one extreme.”
- “Separate facts from assumptions.”

Bad support answers the task:
- giving the exact response;
- exposing the hidden solution;
- listing all arguments the learner should use.

## 9. Challenge rules

A good challenge adds a second conversational condition:
- new information;
- audience change;
- register change;
- objection;
- time pressure;
- forced compromise;
- banned easy word;
- perspective shift;
- extra constraint;
- unexpected follow-up.

Avoid empty challenges such as “Explain more” unless timing itself is the mechanic.

## 10. Activity-specific generation rules

| Activity | New items must preserve this mechanic |
| --- | --- |
| Odd One Out — Conversation Edition | Four items with a defensible relationship and at least one plausible alternative interpretation; avoid trivia-only categories. |
| Would You Rather — No Easy Answers | Genuine trade-off where both choices have costs; avoid obviously good vs obviously bad. |
| One Minute, No Escape | Topic deep enough for sustained speech plus a useful constraint. |
| Explain It Without Saying It | Target plus 2–4 forbidden words that force circumlocution without making it impossible. |
| Bad Advice Only | Relatable problem where intentionally bad advice can lead to useful repair/discussion. |
| Story Chain — But Something Changes | Strong story seed or twist that can be integrated into an existing narrative. |
| Convince Me | Clear persuasion objective with space for objection handling. |
| The Missing Detail | One important missing detail the learner must identify or ask about. |
| Upgrade That Answer | Short/basic answer that can be improved through specificity, reasons, examples or chunks. |
| Three Questions Deeper | Normal opening question that supports increasingly connected deeper follow-ups. |
| Conversation Roulette | Specific but broad prompts that invite personal answers without requiring sensitive disclosure. |
| Defend the Opposite | Position with two defendable sides; not a factual question with one correct answer. |
| Repair the Conversation | Line that is pragmatically awkward, too direct, unclear or unnatural and can be repaired in context. |
| Agree, Disagree, It Depends | Statement with room for qualification; “it depends” must name the condition. |
| What Happened Just Before? | Intriguing final moment with multiple plausible backstories. |
| Make It Sound Like a Person | Understandable but unnatural English with a clearly more idiomatic alternative. |
| Sell Me Something Useless | Difficult product/service paired with an audience whose needs make persuasion non-obvious. |
| The Missing Question | Answer that allows one or more natural questions; avoid answers so broad that anything fits. |
| Take a Side | Two meaningful poles on one continuum; midpoint must also be defendable. |
| Change My Mind | Position that can be challenged with reasons, evidence, examples and concessions. |
| The Better Question | Questions where appropriacy/naturalness differs; not only obvious grammar mistakes. |
| What Would You Say? | Real situation with a concrete interpersonal objective and no single script. |
| Say It Three Ways | One communicative intention that genuinely changes across casual, neutral and professional register. |
| Keep It Going | Conversational line with several connected follow-ups; train reaction + development. |
| The Awkward Silence | Shared context clear enough to restart naturally without random-topic questions. |
| What's the Problem? | Student sees symptoms only; teacher_note contains hidden root cause; questions are needed to uncover it. |
| You Have 30 Seconds | Concrete task small enough for timed retrieval but rich enough to sustain 30–60 seconds. |
| One Detail Is False | Storytelling category that supports believable connected details and follow-up. |
| Build the Perfect... | Construct an ideal version from explicit dimensions, then add constraint/trade-off. |
| Trade-Off | Four to six desirable options but learner may keep only a subset; no universally irrelevant option. |
| Emergency English | Practical high-pressure situation with a specific outcome and escalating complication. |
| The Complaint Ladder | Same problem must work at polite → firm → final-escalation levels. |
| Don’t Say Yes | Question that tempts a binary answer but supports a natural fuller response. |
| Five Whys | Preference/decision/opinion that can deepen into more precise reasons without becoming intrusive. |
| Make It More Specific | Start vague; upgrade requires evidence, examples, behaviour, numbers or precise language. |
| Finish My Thought | Stem that naturally produces a complete personal or hypothetical thought. |
| What Are You Assuming? | Claim with identifiable hidden assumptions; not merely an opinion. |
| Unpopular Opinion | Low-stakes, non-inflammatory topic; challenge is argument quality, not provocation. |
| Explain the Difference | Close lexical/conceptual pair; require contexts/examples, not dictionary definitions only. |
| Which One Sounds More Natural? | Understandable alternatives where idiomaticity, collocation or register differs. |
| The Forbidden Easy Word | Bans that force precision while leaving enough language to complete the task. |
| Use These 3 Chunks | Three chunks that can naturally coexist in one coherent response. |
| Personalise It | Generic statement that must become a concrete personal or invented example. |
| Guess My Rule | teacher_note defines a precise hidden rule plus enough consistent examples for inference. |
| Who Said It? | One line with clues about relationship, context, intention or register. |
| Before / During / After | Event with meaningful preparation, live action and follow-up phases. |
| Problem → Options → Decision | Require problem definition, at least three options, comparison and justified decision. |
| Interrupt Me Politely | Exact reason to interrupt: clarification, correction, redirect, timing, decision, etc. |
| Tell Me What I Mean | Indirect language whose intended meaning depends on context, tone or relationship. |
| Bad Small Talk / Good Small Talk | Contrast conversation mechanics, not “wrong grammar vs correct grammar”. |
| Describe Without Adjectives | Target describable through behaviour, actions, events or sensory detail. |
| Make It Less Direct | Start needlessly forceful; preserve clarity when softening. |
| Make It More Direct | Start too vague/hedged; improve clarity without making it rude. |
| Conversation Fork | One conversational moment plus 2–3 genuinely different strategic directions. |
| The Unexpected Follow-Up | Familiar first question + second question that forces a new angle, not simply “why?”. |
| Explain Your Choice to Someone Who Disagrees | Define listener’s competing value so learner must reframe rather than repeat. |
| Micro Roleplay | One scenario, one objective, 60–90 seconds; challenge complicates without replacing the task. |
| Phrase Auction | Five to seven phrases of different usefulness/register; weak options need not all be ungrammatical. |
| Conversation Detective | Short dialogue fragment with clues; infer relationship, backstory and likely next step. |

## 11. Delivery rule

Generate according to this guide and deliver the final batch as a downloadable JSON file matching the import contract. Do not output a copyable prompt.

## 12. Review checklist

Reject an item if any answer is no:
- Does it preserve the game mechanic?
- Would it create actual speaking?
- Is it meaningfully different from existing items?
- Are its levels plausible?
- Are context tags accurate?
- Are language targets pedagogically meaningful?
- Does the challenge deepen interaction?
- Is student support non-spoilery?
- Is teacher-only information private?
- Would the prompt look clean on the presentation screen?

The library should become broader and more reusable as it grows, not simply longer.

The item must preserve the named game's mechanic. Do not turn every activity into 'What do you think and why?'.
Student-facing wording must be immediately understandable on a projected/shared screen.
Teacher-only answers, secrets, hidden rules, facilitation notes and reveal-later content must never be embedded in the normal learner prompt.
Support gives a route into the task; it must not solve the task.
A challenge changes the communicative demand, information, constraint, role, priority or interaction pattern. 'Say more' is not a challenge.
A batch must contain genuine variation in context, language demand and response path.
Do not use difficulty or CEFR as decoration. They must reflect the actual speaking demand.
For structured games, visual/material data belongs in structured fields, never encoded as pseudo-layout inside text.

authoring_workflow.name: Identify the exact activity and requested levels
instructions: Use the exact activity title already present in the Speaking Library.
Do not rename an existing activity in the import payload.
Determine whether the request is for standard prompt items or one of the five structured formats.
If multiple levels are requested, decide whether each item genuinely works at more than one level; do not attach every requested level to every item automatically.

authoring_workflow.name: Define the speaking behaviour before writing the prompt
instructions: Write down the learner action mentally: ask, clarify, infer, persuade, negotiate, narrate, repair, compare, soften, interrupt, paraphrase, disagree, speculate, etc.
The speaking behaviour must be observable in the learner's response.
If the item can be answered with one isolated word and the game is not intentionally A0-level, the item is probably under-designed.

authoring_workflow.name: Build the scenario and information structure
instructions: Give only the information needed to create a clear communicative problem or choice.
Prefer concrete details, roles, constraints and consequences over broad topic labels.
For lower levels, reduce linguistic complexity before reducing communicative purpose.
For higher levels, add pragmatic, discourse or decision complexity rather than merely adding rare vocabulary.

authoring_workflow.name: Write student-facing text
instructions: Write directly to the learner using short, natural instructions.
Avoid teacher-facing meta-language such as 'elicit', 'drill', 'check understanding' or 'model answer'.
Do not expose the answer, hidden rule, secret option, private cue or intended interpretation.
Keep screen text scannable. Break complex tasks into structured fields rather than one oversized paragraph.

authoring_workflow.name: Add support only where it improves access
instructions: A0-A1 support can include sentence frames, question stems, mini word banks and chunks.
A2-B1 support should usually provide useful language or an interaction route rather than a near-complete answer.
B2-C2 support should be selective and can focus on discourse moves, register, nuance or strategic phrases.
Do not add support mechanically to every item if it is not needed.

authoring_workflow.name: Design a meaningful second stage
instructions: Use a challenge when a reveal or complication can make the same item worth continuing.
Good challenge types: new constraint, new stakeholder, changed priority, contradiction, time pressure, role swap, extra evidence, tone shift, or required follow-up.
The challenge must not invalidate the original task or require information the learner could not reasonably infer.

authoring_workflow.name: Write private teacher guidance
instructions: Use teacher_note or structured teacher fields for answers, accepted interpretations, hidden rules, secret choices, likely alternatives, facilitation moves and ambiguity notes.
Teacher guidance should help run the interaction; it should not over-script the teacher.
For open-ended tasks, describe acceptable response territory rather than pretending there is one exact answer.

authoring_workflow.name: Tag and level the item
instructions: Choose CEFR levels from the allowed list only.
Use 1-4 stable context tags and 1-4 pedagogical language targets.
Set difficulty 1-5 from cognitive/pragmatic demand, not from how sophisticated the topic sounds.

authoring_workflow.name: Run the novelty and batch-balance check
instructions: Compare against supplied existing items and against other items in the same generated batch.
Reject paraphrases and cosmetic noun swaps.
Check context spread, level spread, interaction pattern and response-path variation.
Reorder naturally; do not always progress from easiest to hardest.

authoring_workflow.name: Validate delivery
instructions: Return the exact speaking_item_batch top-level structure.
Do not invent IDs, timestamps, database keys or sequence numbers.
Do not wrap JSON in markdown.
When requested for use in Sblocco, produce one downloadable .json file only.

pedagogical_quality_standard.target_experience: The learner should feel that they are doing something with English, not proving that they know English.
required_characteristics: Enough information or friction to create spoken output.
A response path that cannot be completed by mechanically reading the prompt back.
Language demand appropriate to the assigned level(s).
A reason to listen to the other speaker where the mechanic is interactive.
A scenario that is plausible or intentionally playful, but not arbitrary.

output_depth_targets.A0: Usually 1-4 short chunks or very short exchanges, with strong lexical/visual support.
output_depth_targets.A1: Short but complete utterances and simple question-answer interaction; often 2-5 turns.
output_depth_targets.A1+: Short connected responses with simple reasons, alternatives or follow-ups.
output_depth_targets.A2: Several connected sentences or a short exchange with clarification, reason, comparison or sequence.
output_depth_targets.B1: Sustained explanation or interaction with reasons, examples, follow-up and adaptation.
output_depth_targets.B1+: More flexible spontaneous interaction, clearer discourse structure and less reliance on scaffolds.
output_depth_targets.B2: Nuanced argument, negotiation, register control, inference or extended spontaneous response.
output_depth_targets.C1: Strategic, precise and flexible discourse with implied meaning, reframing, stakeholder awareness or complex interaction.
output_depth_targets.C2: Highly controlled, subtle, rhetorically adaptive or pragmatically demanding speaking; avoid artificial obscurity.
output_depth_targets.Mixed: The mechanic must remain playable across levels. Build optional support/challenge layers instead of averaging everything into bland B1.

reject_if: The item is essentially a grammar worksheet with 'say your answer' added.
The learner can answer well with yes/no and no further requirement.
The task depends on obscure trivia or specialist knowledge unrelated to the language goal.
The only novelty is swapping a person, city, product or object in an otherwise identical prompt.
The task demands personal disclosure about trauma, finances, health, relationships or identity without an easy hypothetical alternative.
The teacher note merely repeats the prompt.
The challenge says only 'speak for longer', 'give more details' or an equivalent empty instruction.
The assigned level is justified mainly by one difficult word.

A0.learner_profile: Very limited productive English. Recognition may be stronger than spontaneous production.
design: Use visible choices, concrete nouns, actions, numbers, people, places and high-frequency chunks.
One communicative decision at a time.
Keep instructions extremely short and preferably model the response shape through support.
Use imagery whenever it genuinely reduces language-processing load.
Allow pointing/choosing plus a spoken chunk rather than requiring unsupported full sentences.
support: visual labels when the mechanic permits them
avoid: tasks requiring tense control the learner has not acquired

A1.learner_profile: Can manage familiar everyday exchanges with simple present/past/future chunks and basic questions.
design: Use familiar scenarios but give a real reason to ask, choose, correct or explain.
Keep sentence structure simple while allowing the communicative goal to remain adult.
Use numbers, schedules, shopping, preferences, directions, routines and simple service situations carefully without making every item childlike.
avoid: four or five constraints at once

A1+.learner_profile: Can extend A1 exchanges with basic reasons, sequencing and simple comparison.
design: Introduce one meaningful complication or follow-up.
Ask for because, but, first/then, better/worse, can/can't style expansion.
Encourage short interaction rather than one-shot answers.

A2.learner_profile: Can handle routine situations and describe, compare, plan and explain familiar matters with some detail.
design: Use realistic choices and small trade-offs.
Require reasons, examples, clarification or sequencing.
Build 30-90 seconds of speaking potential without needing advanced vocabulary.
Use roleplay objectives rather than scripts.
avoid: purely broad conversation questions with no task

B1.learner_profile: Can sustain familiar and semi-unfamiliar interaction, explain reasons and narrate connected events.
design: Use decisions, negotiation, storytelling, repair, persuasion and inferred meaning.
Require adaptation after a follow-up or changed condition.
Allow more than one defensible answer.
Introduce useful chunks/phrasal verbs when natural.
support: ways to buy time or clarify
avoid: tasks where a memorised opinion paragraph is enough

B1+.learner_profile: Transitional upper-intermediate behaviour: more spontaneous, flexible and interactional than standard B1.
design: Reduce scaffold density.
Add pragmatic choices, perspective shift, competing priorities or more demanding follow-up.
Expect clearer discourse organisation and active conversational management.
avoid: B2/C1 abstraction without enough conceptual support

B2.learner_profile: Can interact fluently across a wide range of topics and manage argument, nuance and register with reasonable control.
design: Use competing values, stakeholder needs, implied meaning, persuasion, rebuttal and register.
Require the learner to respond to another person's position rather than deliver a monologue only.
Use realistic professional/social ambiguity.

C1.learner_profile: Can use language flexibly and effectively for complex social, professional and academic purposes.
design: Build strategic communication: reframing, diplomacy, implication, tone control, stakeholder management, complex negotiation.
Make the difficulty come from communicative judgement and discourse control.
Allow multiple plausible interpretations and require evidence.

C2.learner_profile: Can communicate with very high precision, flexibility and sensitivity to nuance.
design: Use subtle register shifts, compressed implied meaning, rhetorical strategy, ambiguity management and high-stakes-but-safe communication.
Keep scenarios natural enough that sophisticated language has a reason to exist.
Require adaptation to listener, context and consequences.
avoid: specialist domain knowledge as a language test

Mixed.learner_profile: Used when the same mechanic can scale naturally across a mixed group or broad library context.
design: Keep the core task accessible.
Provide optional support for lower levels and optional challenge for higher levels.
Do not write one median-level prompt and label it Mixed without actual scalability.
avoid: requiring everyone to perform at the highest level represented

text.purpose: The presentation-ready prompt or scenario. It is also used for search/history matching.
rules: Must make sense without teacher reconstruction.
Must state the learner's communicative job clearly.
May contain line breaks or explicit BAD:/GOOD: sections only when the activity mechanic calls for them.
Should not contain hidden answers, private rules or teacher instructions.

levels.purpose: Declares the levels for which the same item is genuinely usable.
rules: At least one level.
Use an array even for one level.
Do not attach adjacent levels automatically if the speaking demand does not fit both.

student_support.purpose: Optional scaffold for standard prompt items.
rules: Help the learner start or continue.
Do not provide a full answer.
Prefer chunks, stems, categories or strategic prompts.

challenge.type: string OR structured object for structured rounds
rules: Must change the task in a real way.
Do not leak it into the main prompt.
For structured rounds use {text, reveal:'teacher-controlled'}.

teacher_note.purpose: Private facilitation guidance, solution, hidden rule, acceptable interpretation or correction cue.
rules: Never phrase it as student-facing text.
For open tasks describe acceptable directions rather than one fake exact answer.

context_tags.purpose: Stable reusable scenario/context labels for search and coverage.
rules: lowercase
short
reuse existing vocabulary when possible
do not use full phrases as tags

language_targets.purpose: Pedagogical functions or language behaviours practised by the item.
rules: Use functional/pedagogical labels.
Avoid vague tags like english or speaking.
Do not confuse topic with language target.

difficulty.purpose: Relative cognitive/pragmatic demand inside the library.
rules: Independent from CEFR.
Consider ambiguity, number of constraints, interaction pressure, register and perspective shift.

image_url.purpose: Optional single visual asset for a standard speaking item.
rules: Use a real provided asset path/URL.
Requires image_alt.
Do not duplicate teacher-only information in the image or alt text.
Required when image_url is present.
Describe only visible information.
Never reveal a hidden answer or teacher cue.

visuals.purpose: Optional small set of labelled visuals such as BEFORE/AFTER or WHO/WHERE/ACTION.
rules: Use 2-4 visuals.
Each entry uses url, alt and optional label.
Use real assets only.
Keep the set small enough to remain readable.

structured_common_fields.format: Exact structured format id. Must be one of number_mission, picture_detective, explain_without_saying, conversation_detective, make_the_choice.
structured_common_fields.title: Short learner-facing title. Specific enough to distinguish the round; avoid technical labels.
structured_common_fields.instructions: Direct learner instruction explaining what to do, not how the software works.
structured_common_fields.situation: Optional shared scenario context. Use when it materially helps the interaction.
structured_common_fields.outcome: What successful communication achieves. Prefer an observable outcome.
structured_common_fields.support: Array of learner-visible chunks/strategies, not answers.
structured_common_fields.challenge: {text, reveal:'teacher-controlled'}. Reveal is system-normalized; do not invent other reveal modes.
structured_common_fields.role_swap: {enabled:boolean, instruction:string}. If enabled, the second round must still make communicative sense.
structured_common_fields.roles: Usually learner + teacher. Each role has key, name, goal, private_cue. private_cue is teacher-only and is stripped from learner rendering.
structured_common_fields.teacher: Format-specific teacher-only object. Exact accepted fields are defined in structured_format_specs.

visibility_and_privacy.principle: The teacher and learner do not receive identical information. Author private information explicitly so Sblocco can keep it off the student screen.
student_safe_fields: role names and public role goals
structured material intended for the game
teacher_only_fields: structured teacher object fields such as private_cue, secret_option_key, model_response, hidden_clue, interpretation, complication and role_note
the text of a reveal-later challenge until the teacher explicitly reveals it
author_rules: Never duplicate teacher-only information in text, title, instructions, situation, outcome, support or visible material.
Do not write 'the answer is...' in student-visible fields.
In Picture Detective, image_alt must describe only what is visibly in the image; it must not reveal which option is secret.
In Conversation Detective, the dialogue must contain enough evidence to support inference without exposing teacher.interpretation.
If a challenge is intended as a reveal, author it only in challenge.text, not in instructions.

support_design_guide.objective: Reduce access difficulty without reducing the speaking decision to imitation.
strong_support_examples: One advantage is … / The problem is …
Is it something you use at home?
I’m not sure I agree because …
weak_support_examples: The correct answer is option B.
Say: I want a refund because the product is broken.

by_level.A0-A1: Concrete words, fixed chunks, binary choices, sentence frames and question stems are appropriate.
by_level.A2-B1: Use functional phrases, connectors and strategic prompts. Leave content generation to the learner.
by_level.B2-C2: Use support sparingly; focus on discourse strategy, register, nuance and rhetorical moves.

challenge_design_guide.objective: Create a worthwhile second speaking stage after the learner has already engaged with the base task.
strong_patterns: Change one important fact and require repair.
Reveal a new constraint or deadline.
Introduce a stakeholder with a competing priority.
Require the learner to switch role or position.
Add contradictory evidence and ask the learner to revise an interpretation.
Change register: friend → customer, colleague → director, casual → formal.
Impose a lexical or timing constraint that changes language choices.
Ask the learner to defend the same decision to someone who values something different.

before_generation: List the exact activity title and requested level(s).
Define at least 3 context clusters for a medium/large batch when the mechanic permits it.
Plan a mix of communicative functions or response paths before writing individual items.
Check any supplied existing catalog before drafting.
distribution_rules: No more than about 30% of a batch should use the same context unless the user explicitly requested a narrow domain.
Do not place all lower-difficulty items first and all harder items last.
Do not use the same grammatical frame repeatedly.
Vary role relationships: peer, customer/staff, friend, colleague, stranger, service provider, manager, neighbour, etc.
Vary interaction: ask, respond, repair, persuade, decide, infer, narrate, reframe, challenge.
Where appropriate, include both everyday and professional contexts without making professional automatically more advanced.

batch_size_guidance.1-10: Every item should feel clearly distinct. Aim for at least 3 contexts where possible.
batch_size_guidance.11-30: Plan context clusters and difficulty spread explicitly. Check response-path repetition after every 5-10 items.
batch_size_guidance.31-120: Use a coverage matrix: level × context × communicative action × difficulty. Re-run duplicate/near-duplicate review in chunks.
batch_size_guidance.120+: Generate in internally reviewed waves rather than one undifferentiated stream. Preserve consistent schema and game mechanic across all waves.

duplicate_definition: Near paraphrase with the same scenario and same learner action.
Same scenario + same language target + same response path with cosmetic substitutions.
Same hidden rule or same set of trade-offs with renamed objects.
Same answer can be reused with negligible adaptation.
acceptable_reuse: The same vocabulary item used for a different communicative function.
The same context used at a different level with genuinely different interactional demand.
The same language target practised in a meaningfully different relationship, consequence or response path.
A deliberate progression where later items transform rather than repeat an earlier task.
preflight_questions: What must the learner actually DO differently here?
What information is new or differently structured?
Would the same answer work for another item in the batch?
Does this item add level, context, pragmatic, lexical or interaction coverage?
If I replace one noun, does the item become another existing item? If yes, rewrite.

number_mission.label: Number Mission
number_mission.pedagogical_purpose: Make numerical information consequential inside a live exchange so the learner must listen, confirm, repair and reach a shared accurate result.

item_shape.label: Short human-readable label such as People, Time, Date, Room, Price, Platform or Code.
item_shape.value: Canonical value. May be string or number.
item_shape.display: Optional learner-friendly rendering such as '7:30 p.m.' or '€48'.
item_shape.kind: quantity | time | weekday | date | price | code | other

teacher_contract.private_cue: Required teacher-only mismatch/read-back cue or information asymmetry that creates the need to listen and repair.
teacher_contract.final_confirmation: Optional teacher-only final state or confirmation.

authoring_rules: Numbers must matter to task success; do not create plain number dictation.
Use at least two separate numerical/details categories.
The teacher cue should create a natural opportunity for clarification or correction.
For A0-A1, prefer visible fact cards and high-frequency repair chunks.
For A2-B1, combine numbers with consequences: booking, schedule, order, deadline, quantity, price, route or plan.
good_challenges: teacher reads one number back incorrectly
reject_if: facts are just a list to read aloud
the teacher cue does not create interaction
all facts are irrelevant decoration

picture_detective.label: Picture Detective
picture_detective.pedagogical_purpose: Use visual information to generate genuine questions, descriptive language, categorisation and hypothesis testing.

material_contract.show_labels: Boolean. Use true for lower-level lexical access when labels do not destroy the mechanic.

item_shape.key: Short unique option key, e.g. A, B, C.
item_shape.label: Name of visible object/person/place/scene.
item_shape.image_url: Final asset path/URL. Required for publishable structured content.
item_shape.image_alt: Accessible visual description that does not reveal the secret.

teacher_contract.secret_option_key: Required. Must exactly match one authored option key.

authoring_rules: Options must be visually or conceptually distinct enough to support useful questions but similar enough that one question does not always solve the task.
For beginners, imagery should carry meaning rather than decorate text.
Do not place the secret in image_alt, label styling, title or support.
Questions should target meaningful attributes: use, location, size, material, category, situation, action.
Avoid culturally obscure objects unless the image itself makes them clear.
good_challenges: describe a new option without naming it
reject_if: one option is obviously different
images are missing
alt text leaks secret
labels make the answer trivial when labels should be hidden

explain_without_saying.label: Explain Without Saying
explain_without_saying.pedagogical_purpose: Develop circumlocution, lexical flexibility and repair by making the learner explain a target without relying on its most obvious lexical shortcuts.

material_contract.target: Word, chunk, concept or expression to communicate.
material_contract.forbidden_words: Array of at least two distinct words that are genuinely useful shortcuts but do not make the task impossible.

teacher_contract.model_response: Optional teacher-only example of one viable explanation. It is not an exact answer key.

authoring_rules: The target itself must not be repeated as a forbidden word.
Forbidden words should force paraphrase, not sabotage the task.
At lower levels, choose concrete targets and fewer high-value bans.
At higher levels, use abstract concepts, professional/social language, chunks or nuanced terms.
Support should suggest semantic routes such as function, situation, consequence, category or example without stating the answer.
good_challenges: give a real example after the guess
explain it to a child/client/new colleague
reject_if: target is impossible to explain without banned words
forbidden list contains obscure unrelated words
model response is exposed to learner

conversation_detective.label: Conversation Detective
conversation_detective.pedagogical_purpose: Train inference from conversational evidence: relationship, intention, shared knowledge, tension, implied meaning, context and likely next action.

material_contract.question: The inference question. It must require evidence from the dialogue.
material_contract.follow_up: Optional visible follow-up that deepens interpretation.

teacher_contract.hidden_clue: Optional private contextual clue for teacher facilitation/reveal.
teacher_contract.interpretation: Required private accepted reading or range of plausible readings.

authoring_rules: Dialogue must sound spoken, not like exposition written to hide a riddle.
Include enough evidence for a defensible inference.
Avoid requiring one culturally specific interpretation when several are equally plausible.
At A2, infer concrete situation/relationship. At B1-B2, infer intention/tension. At C1-C2, use implication, politeness, power, stance or strategic ambiguity.
Teacher interpretation may acknowledge multiple acceptable answers.
good_challenges: add one clue and revise the inference
reject_if: dialogue contains the answer explicitly
question can be answered without reading dialogue
teacher interpretation treats an ambiguous exchange as objectively certain

make_the_choice.label: Make the Choice
make_the_choice.pedagogical_purpose: Create real comparison, prioritisation, negotiation and justification by giving options with defensible but conflicting advantages.

material_contract.situation: Shared decision context and any important global constraint.

item_shape.key: Stable author-facing key; Sblocco can normalize from title.
item_shape.title: Short visible option name.
item_shape.details: At least two {label,value} details per option so the trade-off is visible.

teacher_contract.complication: Optional teacher-only new information/reveal that changes the decision landscape.
teacher_contract.role_note: Optional teacher-only priority or stance for live negotiation.

authoring_rules: Every option must remain defensible for some learner priority.
Use comparable dimensions across options when possible.
Do not create a fake choice with one obviously superior option.
For A1+-A2, use 2-3 concrete criteria. For B1-B2, add competing priorities. For C1, add stakeholder or strategic consequences.
The task should require a spoken decision, not merely reading pros and cons.
good_challenges: a stakeholder rejects the first choice
learner must defend choice to someone who disagrees
reject_if: one option dominates every criterion
details are too vague to compare
options differ only cosmetically

standard_item_examples.why_it_works: Concrete situation + clear communicative purpose + natural learner choice.

item.text: Your hotel room is much noisier than you expected. It is 11 p.m. Call reception, explain the problem and ask for a realistic solution.
item.student_support: The problem is… / Would it be possible to…?
item.challenge: Reception says there are no other rooms tonight. Negotiate another solution.
item.teacher_note: Accept room change, quiet-room request, earplugs/discount/next-day move or other realistic solutions. Encourage polite escalation.

standard_item_examples.why_it_works: The mechanic forces elaboration rather than banning one word arbitrarily.

item.text: Do you usually know what you want to order before you open a menu?
item.student_support: Usually… / It depends… / Most of the time…
item.challenge: Answer the teacher’s next two questions without using yes or no.
item.teacher_note: Follow with questions that naturally invite yes/no, then reward expansion rather than grammar perfection.

standard_item_examples.why_it_works: The clue is inside natural dialogue and the answer requires evidence, not trivia.

item.text: A: 'You don’t have to stay if you’ve got somewhere else to be.' B: 'No, no. I said I’d help. I’m just checking the time.' What is probably happening between them?
item.student_support: Think about what A may be implying and why B immediately explains themself.
item.challenge: Say the same situation again, but make A sound genuinely relaxed instead of slightly annoyed.
item.teacher_note: Likely reading: A senses B wants to leave or is distracted; B reassures them. Other evidence-based readings are acceptable.

ai_forbidden_actions: Do not invent activity IDs, item IDs, learner IDs, UUIDs, database primary keys or foreign keys.
Do not invent sequence indexes, row numbers, timestamps, created_at/updated_at values, versions beyond those explicitly defined in this kit, storage paths or signatures.
Do not invent unsupported structured format ids.
Do not invent reveal modes; structured challenge reveal is teacher-controlled.
Do not add schema fields simply because they seem useful. Use only the import contract plus the structured fields documented here.
Do not embed HTML, React, CSS, markdown tables or layout instructions inside item text.
Do not add answer keys to learner-visible fields.
Do not fabricate image URLs. For Picture Detective, use real provided asset paths if available; otherwise the draft should remain incomplete/repairable rather than pretending an asset exists.
Do not silently drop requested levels or requested item counts.
Do not 'fix' an exact existing activity title by renaming it.
Do not restrict an activity itself to only its recommended levels. Every activity remains available A0-C2.
Do not tag every item A0-C2 merely because the activity supports all levels. Item levels must reflect the actual authored language demand.
Do not add decorative images solely because a game supports images.

general: Use imagery when it reduces language load or is central to the mechanic, especially for beginners.
Do not require colour perception alone to distinguish critical options.
Avoid tiny textual information embedded inside images.
Image-dependent tasks must still have accurate alt text.
picture_detective: Every visible option requires image_url and image_alt before publish.
Alt text should describe visible facts only and must not reveal teacher.secret_option_key.
If labels are shown, labels must help language access without making the detective mechanic pointless.
Prefer images with clear silhouettes and meaningful visual differences at classroom-screen size.

rules: Use adult-respectful scenarios across levels. Beginner does not mean childish.
Vary ages, jobs, living situations and social roles without stereotyping.
Do not assume marriage, children, university, office work, car ownership or international travel.
Avoid forcing disclosure about trauma, abuse, medical history, money problems, religion, politics, sexuality or family conflict.
When a potentially personal topic is pedagogically useful, make a hypothetical or third-person route equally natural.
Avoid humiliating roleplays or scenarios where the learner is pressured to reveal private information.

per_item_gate: If the item has image_url or visuals, are all assets real and all alt texts non-spoiling?
Are item levels honest about the actual language demand rather than copied from the activity-level availability?
per_batch_gate: No more than ~30% same context unless intentionally narrow?
At least 3 context clusters for a normal medium/large general batch?
No repeated teacher-note formula that ignores item specifics?
No systematic ordering from easiest to hardest unless requested?
Higher levels include natural chunks/phrasal verbs where useful, not forced?
Every item would plausibly generate learner speech in a live lesson?
If this is a complete activity pack, does it deliberately cover A0 through C2?
structured_item_gate: Teacher-only fields stored only in teacher/private positions?
Challenge not leaked into visible fields?
Roles usable and role swap coherent?
Picture assets real and accessible if Picture Detective?
Choice options genuinely comparable if Make the Choice?
Dialogue inferable but not explicit if Conversation Detective?
Forbidden words workable if Explain Without Saying?

common_failure_modes.symptom: Different games all become 'What do you think about X? Explain.'
common_failure_modes.repair: Return to the named mechanic and create the information gap, rule, constraint or interaction that makes that game unique.

common_failure_modes.symptom: C1 item is an ordinary A2 task with difficult vocabulary.
common_failure_modes.repair: Increase pragmatic/discourse demand: implication, stakeholder conflict, register, reframing, ambiguity or negotiation.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Student support contains nearly the full sentence the learner should produce.
common_failure_modes.repair: Reduce support to chunks, categories, stems or strategic prompts.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Challenge says 'give another reason' or 'speak for longer'.
common_failure_modes.repair: Change information, constraint, audience, role, priority or evidence.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Answer or hidden rule appears in text, instructions, image alt, support or situation.
common_failure_modes.repair: Move it to teacher_note or the structured teacher object and rewrite visible fields.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Ten prompts share the same response path with different nouns/cities/products.
common_failure_modes.repair: Change learner action, relationship, stakes, information structure or language target.

common_failure_modes.symptom: A0/A1 content becomes childish rather than linguistically accessible.
common_failure_modes.repair: Keep adult scenarios but reduce linguistic load and add imagery/chunks.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Number cards, image options or comparison tables are written manually into text.
common_failure_modes.repair: Use the format-specific material fields so Sblocco can render the correct layout.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Make the Choice has a clearly superior choice.
common_failure_modes.repair: Rebalance costs/benefits so different priorities can lead to different defensible choices.

common_failure_modes.symptom: Conversation Detective depends on arbitrary hidden trivia.
common_failure_modes.repair: Put meaningful conversational evidence in the dialogue and allow evidence-based alternatives.

Agree, Disagree, It Depends.core_mechanic: Use a claim with enough nuance for agreement, disagreement or a conditional position. Avoid one-fact questions.
Agree, Disagree, It Depends.must_include: A claim with genuine room for agreement, disagreement or a conditional answer.
Agree, Disagree, It Depends.learner_action: Take a position, explain conditions and react to challenge.
Agree, Disagree, It Depends.support_guidance: Offer language that helps the learner enter the task without supplying the substantive answer.

final_self_review_algorithm: Read the activity title. State the mechanic in one sentence. If your items do not visibly implement it, rewrite.
For every item, state the learner's main spoken action using one verb. If the verb is only 'answer', make the task more specific.
Check student-visible fields for teacher secrets/answers.
Check support: delete anything that gives away the response.
Check challenge: delete or rewrite any challenge that does not materially change the task.
Check levels against the CEFR guide. Remove levels that require too much or too little support.
Compare every item with every other item in the batch for response-path duplication.
Count items and level coverage exactly.
For structured rounds, validate every required material/teacher field against structured_format_specs.
Output only the importable JSON batch when the user asks for the downloadable authoring result.

lower_level_game_pack.purpose: Ten lower-level-first games designed for A0–A2 1:1 speaking with high interaction and low reading load.
design_rules: Beginner does not mean childish: contexts stay adult and practical.
Prefer visible information, short turns and reusable chunks.
Use numbers, images, choices, repair, sequencing and questions to vary cognitive demand.
A0 may answer with chunks; A1/A2 should progressively connect turns.
Every game must still involve teacher-student interaction rather than silent selection.

activity_level_policy.principle: Every Speaking Library activity is available at every learner level from A0 through C2. Activity availability and item authoring level are different concepts.
activity_level_policy.recommended_levels_mean: Recommended levels indicate where the mechanic is especially high-value. They are a ranking signal, never a gate.
activity_level_policy.item_levels_mean: Each item keeps the exact CEFR level(s) it was authored for. Do not relabel an A1 prompt as C2 simply to create coverage.
activity_level_policy.fallback_behavior: If a selected activity has no exact item for the requested level, Sblocco may use the nearest authored level set so the game remains playable. This is a compatibility fallback, not permission to author vague all-level items.
activity_level_policy.full_catalog_rule: When expanding an activity as a complete content pack, deliberately create appropriate items across A0, A1, A1+, A2, B1, B1+, B2, C1 and C2.
activity_level_policy.mixed: Mixed is a delivery context, not a CEFR level. Use layered support/challenge rather than replacing exact item levels with Mixed.

image_support_contract.principle: Images are pedagogical input, not decoration. Use them when they reduce reading load, create an information gap, provide evidence, or are intrinsic to the mechanic.

standard_item_fields.image_url: Optional path/URL for one learner-visible image.
standard_item_fields.image_alt: Required whenever image_url is present. Describe visible information without leaking teacher-only answers.
standard_item_fields.image_label: Optional short learner-visible caption for the single image.
standard_item_fields.visuals: Optional array for 2-4 learner-visible visuals. Each entry uses {url, alt, label}. Use this instead of image_url for BEFORE/AFTER, WHO/WHERE/ACTION, or comparable visual sets.

categories.required: New items for this game should include images because the mechanic depends on visual information. Legacy text items remain runnable while being upgraded.
categories.recommended: Prefer images, especially at A0-A1, because they materially reduce language-processing load or strengthen the mechanic.
categories.optional: Images can create useful variants but should not be forced into every item.
categories.none: The mechanic is primarily linguistic/pragmatic. Do not add decorative images by default.
